query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor concentration of yttrium to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, lubricious, and thermally stable Y-rich oxide tribofilm across the entire temperature range, thereby reducing the coefficient of friction and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with known sliding behavior that includes rising friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to unstable oxide scale formation.
generation.intervention: Alloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with a low concentration (approximately 0.5–2 wt.%) of yttrium during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests performed in a dry ambient environment under a representative load (e.g., 5–10 N in pin-on-disk experiments) across temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The key structural mediator is the Y-rich oxide scale that forms on the worn surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature sliding, yttrium atoms segregate to the surface and oxidize preferentially to form a continuous, adherent Y-rich oxide layer. This lubricious layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby decreasing friction and wear. At lower temperatures, the small amount of yttrium does not adversely affect the inherent mechanical properties of the alloy, while still providing sufficient segregation under sliding conditions to initiate oxide formation as temperature increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the yttrium-doped variant is predicted to maintain a consistently lower coefficient of friction and exhibit reduced wear throughout the range of temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, which shows increased friction and accelerated wear at higher temperatures due to less effective oxide scale formation.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits apply under controlled, dry sliding conditions with loads in the specified range. The performance might vary under drastically different environmental conditions (e.g., high humidity, lubricated contacts) or under loads significantly beyond those tested.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty concerning the optimal yttrium concentration to balance low-temperature mechanical properties and high-temperature tribological performance. Also, the long-term stability of the Y-rich oxide layer under cyclic or extended sliding in real-world applications is not fully known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi specimens: one doped with approximately 1 wt.% yttrium and one undoped (baseline). Conduct systematic pin-on-disk sliding tests over a temperature range from RT to 800 °C under identical load and environmental conditions, while monitoring friction behavior and wear track evolution.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Wear track depth and morphology assessed by profilometry and scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Surface composition and presence of Y-rich oxide scales evaluated using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the yttrium-doped samples do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower friction coefficients and reduced wear) across the temperature range compared to the undoped alloy, or if no continuous Y-rich oxide scale is observed on the sliding interfaces.
